title: Reduced striatal dopamine transporter density in abstinent methamphetamine and methcathinone users: Evidence from positron emission tomography studies with [11C]WIN-35,428

claims.statement: In adults with a history of heavy methamphetamine use, scanned after days to months of abstinence, striatal dopamine transporter availability is lower on average than in people who do not use: about 20–28% lower in individual PET studies, and a pooled standardized difference of g = −1.47 (95% CI −1.83 to −1.10; 9 studies, 108 users, 126 controls). Individual values overlap with the control range, and these designs cannot show whether the difference reflects lost nerve terminals, reduced transporter expression or differences that predate use.
claims.magnitude: Individual PET studies: caudate −27.8% and putamen −21.1% (15 users vs 18 controls); caudate −23% and putamen −25% (6 vs 10). Pooled: g −1.47 (95% CI −1.83 to −1.10), 9 studies of amphetamine-type stimulant users. Group distributions overlap.

claims.statement: Whether methamphetamine use, as people use it, causes lasting loss of or damage to dopamine neurons in humans has not been established: lower dopamine markers in heavy users are consistently found, but the measures available cannot distinguish loss of nerve terminals from reversible down-regulation, some markers return toward normal with abstinence, and the pattern differs from that of Parkinson's disease.
claims.magnitude: Not estimable: no study has counted dopamine neurons or terminals quantitatively in human users.
